title: Roof and Wall Exhaust Path Explorer
description: Learners predict the discharge path of seven roof and wall ventilation units from schematic cutaways with the discharge hidden, then see the true path drawn with airflow arrows and the reason. Parts are clickable for definitions, a yes/no question asks whether a gravity relief ventilator needs a fan, and a summary table reopens any unit without changing the score.

educational.audience: Adult professional development: new application engineers, sales staff, representatives and facilities staff
educational.topic: Discharge paths of roof and wall ventilation units
learningObjectives: The learner will classify seven roof and wall ventilation configurations by the path the exhaust air takes as it leaves the unit, given a cutaway of each unit with its discharge hidden.

rules: Seven path items, shuffled once per session, then the gravity question.
Upblast and side wall configurations move air in a straight line; downblast, louvered and hooded configurations move it up, then down and outward (FanPedia p. 5).
The cutaway hides the discharge arrows until the learner commits; the correct path is revealed after every commit.
One attempt per item, no re-answering. Mastery: 6 of 7 paths plus the gravity question, on first attempts.
assumptions: Cutaways are schematic and not to scale; they show only the parts named in the chapter spec.
limitations: Does not show product-specific construction such as motor-out-of-airstream tubes, belt drives or curb sizes; check the current catalog for a product line.

pedagogical.teachingStrategy: Commit a prediction from the unit's construction, then compare it with the revealed airflow path and the reason
keyQuestions: Which part above the impeller decides where the air goes?
Why do the hooded, louvered and downblast units share one path?
What moves the air through a gravity relief ventilator?
commonMisconceptions: Every roof exhauster blows air straight up.
A hood or louvers change the fan type inside the unit.
Downblast units are suitable for any exhaust because the air still leaves the building.
A gravity relief ventilator contains a small fan.
assessmentOpportunities: First-attempt score shown as 'Paths correct: n of 7'; mastery is 6 of 7 paths plus the gravity question, on first attempts.
